To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of fecally derived microorganisms in groundwater used for irrigation is widespread, that fecal bacteria are not reliable indicators of the presence of enteric viruses and that the presence of enteroviruses and rotaviruses in groundwater used for agriculture may pose an infectious risk to farmers.
77.5% of the wells were contaminated with fecal bacteria, and that 15.6% of the wells contained enteric viruses.

58% of groundwater samples were contaminated by fecal bacteria (E. coli, Salmonellae, total coliform bacteria, and enterococcii) and that 15.6% were positive for enteric viruses (noroviruses, rotaviruses and enteroviruses).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the need to develop a new strategy to evaluate the suitability of groundwater for irrigation, based on the detection of enteric viruses.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the water from 58 wells (i.e., 31.9% of the total number of wells analyzed) is potentially contaminated with human pathogens.

the presence of enteric viruses in groundwater used for irrigation should not be overlooked, and that the use of fecal bacteria as indicators for the evaluation of the suitability of groundwater for irrigation purposes is not appropriate.
the presence of enteric viruses in water for irrigation is not predictable from the fecal bacterial indicators, but it should be assessed in order to protect human health.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of enteric viruses as a tool for the assessment of groundwater quality and its suitability for irrigation purposes is recommended.
, in the case of Apulian groundwater, the use of fecal bacteria as indicators of fecal contamination does not guarantee the absence of enteric viruses.
enteric viruses should be included as indicators in the Italian Ministerial Decrees to evaluate the suitability of groundwater for irrigation purposes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of enteric viruses as indicators of groundwater pollution could improve the assessment of water quality for irrigation purposes.
the use of fecal bacteria to assess groundwater quality for irrigation is not adequate and should be improved by the addition of viral analysis.
the presence of viruses in groundwater is not always associated with fecal bacteria indicators and that viruses can be detected in water considered suitable for irrigation purposes.
